questions.prompt: What is the key memory signature of process hollowing?
options: A remote thread with a start address in kernel32.dll
A mismatch between what a process claims to be running (its reported image path) and what's actually mapped at its image base address
A named mutex with a suspicious string
A process running with SYSTEM privileges
questions.explanation: Process hollowing unmaps a legitimate process's original image and writes a different PE into the same address space -- the process looks legitimate at the process level, but what's actually mapped at its image base doesn't match what it claims to be.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't reflective DLL injection appear in a process's normal module list?
options: It's encrypted and hidden from all analysis
It implements its own PE-loading logic rather than calling LoadLibrary, so it never touches disk and never registers through the normal module-loading mechanism
Reflective injection only works on 32-bit systems
It always terminates the process immediately after loading
questions.explanation: Because reflective loading bypasses LoadLibrary entirely -- parsing its own headers, resolving its own imports -- it's mapped in memory but never appears in the self-reported module list, exactly the kind of mismatch ldrmodules is built to catch.

questions.prompt: What makes the "Early Bird" APC injection variant specifically effective at evasion?
options: It only works on outdated Windows versions
It queues the APC before a newly-created process's main thread has even started running, aiming to execute before security tooling that hooks normal startup has a chance to engage
It requires no suspended thread at all
questions.explanation: By queuing the APC before the target's own code starts running, Early Bird aims to execute before security tooling gets a chance to hook into the process's normal startup sequence.

questions.prompt: How does thread execution hijacking differ from the other injection techniques covered in this lesson?
options: It requires creating multiple new threads
It doesn't create anything new -- it suspends an already-running thread, redirects its instruction pointer with SetThreadContext, then resumes it
It only works against suspended processes
It always crashes the target process
questions.explanation: Unlike DLL injection or APC injection, thread execution hijacking never creates a new thread -- it takes an existing, previously legitimate thread and redirects it mid-flight.
